title: Identity Management Platform Guide: How to Choose the Right Security & Compliance Platform
description: Practical identity management platform guidance with planning steps, controls, failure tests, and a readiness checklist.
author: Marcus Rivera

sections.title: Map identities and access paths
sections.body: Inventory employees, contractors, partners, customers, service accounts, and privileged administrators. Record which applications each identity can access, how accounts are created, and who approves exceptions. Include legacy apps and cloud consoles that are not connected to the central identity provider. The goal is to understand where access is duplicated, delayed, or impossible to revoke—not merely to count applications.

sections.title: Define the identity lifecycle
sections.body: Specify joiner, mover, and leaver workflows, including who approves access, how roles are assigned, and how quickly access is removed. Test a role change that requires both granting new permissions and removing old ones. Establish how emergency access works and how exceptions expire. Automating provisioning without clear role definitions can spread excessive access faster than manual processes.

sections.title: Evaluate authentication and federation
sections.body: Test SSO protocols, MFA options, conditional access, device requirements, passwordless methods, and recovery. Include applications with different protocols and users who lose a device or work offline. Verify that disabling an account actually blocks existing sessions and tokens where required. Document which systems still use local credentials and how those exceptions are monitored.

sections.title: Govern privileged access
sections.body: Separate everyday accounts from administrative accounts and require stronger controls for high-impact systems. Test approval workflows, just-in-time access if available, session visibility, credential rotation, and emergency recovery. Limit who can change identity policies and protect the break-glass account. Ensure audit records can explain who granted access, what changed, and why.

sections.title: Connect directories and applications safely
sections.body: Map HRIS, directories, SaaS apps, cloud infrastructure, customer identity, and service accounts. Test duplicate identities, renamed users, external domains, group changes, and failed provisioning. Use scoped credentials for integrations and define retry and alert behavior. Avoid allowing multiple systems to overwrite the same attributes without a clear authority rule.

sections.title: Review compliance and privacy needs
sections.body: Identify which access events, authentication records, and user attributes are logged and how long they are retained. Restrict access to identity logs and exports. Verify regional data handling, audit retention, and contractual terms against the organization's requirements. A vendor's certification does not automatically establish that a particular configuration satisfies every regulatory obligation.

sections.title: Measure access hygiene
sections.body: Track application coverage, stale accounts, provisioning failures, time to revoke access, privileged exceptions, MFA coverage, and access-review completion. Set an owner and response target for each high-risk exception. Use the metrics to reduce exposure rather than create a dashboard nobody acts on.

sections.title: Selection checklist
sections.body: Pilot with representative users and applications. Verify lifecycle automation, authentication, recovery, least privilege, audit evidence, integration failures, and offboarding. Keep an inventory of exceptions and review them regularly. Reassess when the application estate, workforce model, or threat profile changes.

sections.title: Run an access review and recovery drill
sections.body: Test joiner, mover, and leaver scenarios across representative applications, including a contractor whose end date changes and an employee who changes teams. Verify that access is granted only after approval, removed within the required window, and logged with the reason. Simulate a failed directory sync and a lost administrator account to confirm recovery steps. Measure stale accounts, excessive privileges, and time to revoke access instead of judging success by the number of connected applications.
